newsitem.title: QATAR: Gulf states still differ on unified tariffs.
newsitem.headline: Gulf states still differ on unified tariffs.

text.p: Gulf Arab states are still struggling to agree on unified custom tariffs which would help them form a common market and open doors to free trade with major economic blocs, delegates at a Gulf summit said on Sunday.
"I do not think we will have an agreement at this summit," said one delegate. "There is a difference in ideology".
The summit has been boycotted by Bahrain over a territorial dispute with Qatar.
The Gulf Cooperation Council states -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, Qatar amd the United Arab Emirates -- have been discussing unifying their tariffs for over 10 years.

GCC finance and economy ministers held talks late into the night on Saturday on the sidelines of the three-day summit to resolve differences over tariffs, but the delegates said no final solution was reached.
They were due to resume talks on Sunday, the third session in two days, while their leaders will hold formal summit talks on broad political, economic and military issues on the agenda.
"The summit could postpone a decision (on tariffs) to the next one in Kuwait" in late 1997, said one delegate.
Any agreement should be reviewed by GCC foreign ministers before it is presented to the summit.

The UAE, a major regional trading and re-export centre, is reluctant to raise tariffs beyond the four to six percent level which is imposed on most goods while Saudi Arabia, which has tariffs of 20 percent on a range of goods, is in favour of a unified GCC level of 8-12 percent on most goods.
Saudi Arabia accounts for about 40 percent of total GCC imports of about $68 billion a year.

The six states sit on 45 percent of the world's oil reserves and have built an impressive petrochemical industry. They need to unify tariffs to jump-start more than 10 years of talks with the European Union on a free trade accord which could open European markets to cheap GCC petrochemicals.
Foreign ministers of the GCC and the EU agreed in April on a time frame of no more than two years to complete the deal.
Qatari newspapers said Qatar, the current GCC chairman, would concentrate its efforts on achieving real economic GCC integration.
Qatari Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani urged the summit in an opening speech on Saturday to double efforts to remove all trade restrictions and barriers among the GCC states.
